opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so at the time, in 2012, I was at NYU working with Yann LeCun's group, with Pierre Sermanet, and we were working on the Street View House Numbers dataset. The way most of the computer vision community approached a problem like that was a pipeline: you'd take your images, run some carefully engineered feature extractor over them, like SIFT, HOG, or some variant of gradient histograms, maybe pool those into a bag-of-words representation, and then train a classifier on top, usually an SVM. All the human cleverness went into designing that feature extractor. People spent years of PhDs tuning how you bin the gradients, how you normalize, what the cell sizes are.

The way I understood the difference, and honestly the way Yann had been preaching it for twenty years, was that the convnet just learns the features. You give it raw pixels, maybe with a bit of normalization, and the whole thing is trained end to end with backprop. The early layers end up learning things that look like edge detectors and Gabor-like filters, which is roughly what the handcrafted people were designing by hand anyway, but the network figures out what's actually useful for *your* task and *your* data, and it learns the higher-level compositions too, which is very hard to hand-design.

In that paper we also played with things like multi-stage features, feeding the first-stage features directly into the classifier alongside the second-stage ones, and Lp pooling instead of plain max or average pooling. Those were small architectural ideas, but the bigger point was philosophical: stop engineering the representation, engineer the learning system and let data and compute do the rest.

And to be honest, I didn't fully appreciate how big that shift was at the time. I was a pretty junior person just trying to get numbers to go up. In hindsight it was a front-row seat to the moment the field flipped. Later that same year AlexNet came out on ImageNet and suddenly everyone else saw it too.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts handcrafted feature extractors with a ConvNet trained end to end from raw pixels.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, I should correct the premise a bit, because that paper wasn't mine. The 2012 result everyone means is AlexNet, from Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoff Hinton. I was a grad student in Yann LeCun's lab at NYU around then, so I was very much in the audience for it, not on the author list. But that result shaped everything I did afterwards, so I'm happy to talk about how it landed.

The way I understood it at the time was pretty simple. The vision pipeline that dominated was: a human designs a feature detector, SIFT or HOG or some variant, you pool those features somehow, maybe build a bag-of-words or a Fisher vector on top, and then you train a shallow classifier like an SVM on the result. Years of PhD effort went into that first stage. People's entire careers were about finding a slightly better descriptor. The learning only happened at the very end, on top of representations that were frozen by design.

The ConvNet flipped the question. Instead of asking "what features should I compute," it asked "what features would fall out if I just let the gradient decide." The architecture encodes some priors, locality, weight sharing, a bit of translation invariance, but it doesn't hard-code edges or gradients or orientation histograms. You hand it pixels and a label and the whole stack, from the first layer to the classifier, gets trained jointly. That joint training is the key thing. The low-level features are shaped by what the high-level task actually needs, rather than by what a human guessed would be useful.

And honestly, people in Yann's lab had believed this for a long time. The idea wasn't new. What was new in 2012 was that it finally won by a margin nobody could argue with, on a benchmark everybody cared about. The handcrafted-feature people had been slowly grinding ImageNet error down by a point or two a year, and then a ConvNet shows up and cuts it by something like ten points. That's not an incremental improvement, that's a different regime.

The other thing I remember being struck by was how much of it came down to engineering rather than a new idea. GPUs, enough data, ReLUs so the thing would actually train deep, dropout so it wouldn't overfit. None of those individually was a conceptual breakthrough. It was the first time all the pieces were in the same room at once. And that lesson, that making the tooling good enough is itself the research, is a lot of why I ended up spending the next decade on Torch and then PyTorch instead of on another descriptor.

r001.rationale: It contrasts hand-designed features with training the entire ConvNet jointly from pixels and labels, identifying end-to-end learning as the alternative.

astra-6.text:
The central difference was where the features came from. In the traditional pipeline, you would design a feature extractor—something like SIFT or HOG—and then train a classifier on top. Learning was happening, but the representation was largely fixed by the person designing the system.

With a ConvNet, you learned the representation together with the classifier, directly from the pixels. The training objective could change the filters throughout the network, so the features became specific to the task. You were still putting in assumptions through the architecture, like locality and weight sharing, but you weren’t specifying which visual patterns it should detect.

So, to me, the shift was from engineering the features to engineering a system that could learn the features.

r001.rationale: It says ConvNets learned the representation and classifier directly from pixels, contrasting this with manually designed features such as SIFT or HOG.

sol-6.1.text:
The central difference was what you learned versus what you designed by hand. In the traditional pipeline, you would design a feature extractor—say, SIFT or HOG—and then train a classifier on those features. A lot of the intelligence was in the researcher deciding what information the representation should preserve.

With a ConvNet, you learned the representation along with the classifier, directly from pixels. You still made design choices about the architecture, but you weren’t specifying the visual features yourself. The training objective could shape every layer toward the task.

And that changed how you could make progress. Instead of having to invent a better feature descriptor, you could ask whether more data, more computation, or a better way of training would let the model learn a better representation.

r001.rationale: It contrasts manually designed features such as SIFT or HOG with a ConvNet learning the representation and classifier directly from pixels.
